lessons.title: Bid, Ask, Spread and Pips: The Hidden Cost of Every Currency Trade

children.text: Kavya buys $1,000 in cash at a forex counter in Chennai before a trip to Singapore. The trip gets cancelled the same afternoon, so she walks back to the same counter and sells the $1,000. She loses ₹3,500 without the rupee moving at all. Nobody cheated her. She paid the spread, the gap between the price a dealer sells at and the price it buys at. Every currency transaction you will ever make, from an airport counter to a USD/INR futures trade on NSE, carries this cost. This lesson teaches you to see it, measure it and shrink it.

body.text: Every currency quote is really two prices. You always buy at the higher one and sell at the lower one, so every trade starts at a small loss. The spread is the price of admission, and the smaller it is, the better the market is for you.

children.text: Bid and Ask: Two Prices, One Quote

markDefs.definition: The price at which a dealer will buy the base currency from you. It is the price you get when you sell.
Also called the offer. The price at which a dealer will sell the base currency to you. It is the price you pay when you buy.
The midpoint between bid and ask. It is the rate you usually see in news headlines and charts, but no one can actually trade at it.

children.text: A dealer always quotes two numbers. The
bid
is what the dealer pays to buy dollars from you. The
ask
is what the dealer charges to sell dollars to you. The ask is always higher. The
mid rate
sits between them, and it is the number you see on TV. Remember it from the dealer's side: the dealer buys low and sells high, and you are on the other side of both.

body.caption: The two numbers every forex quote gives you
The same USD/INR market through four doors (illustrative, mid rate 95.50)

cells: Cash notes at a forex counter

children.text: The futures price is higher than spot because a futures contract settles in the future, and that price includes the interest rate gap between India and the US. You will learn exactly why in the last lesson of this chapter. For now, focus on the spread column. The same dollar costs a bank half a paisa to trade, while Kavya pays ₹3.50 at a cash counter, 700 times more.

body.title: Spread per US Dollar by Channel (paise, illustrative)
Which price do you get?
body.question: Your bank quotes USD/INR TT rates of 94.70 / 96.30. Your US client has just paid you $2,000 and you want to convert it to rupees. At what rate will the bank convert it?
options: Whichever rate is better for you
body.explanation: You are selling dollars, so you get the bank's bid, 94.70. The bank buys low from you and sells high to someone else. You receive $2,000 × 94.70 = ₹1,89,400, compared with ₹1,91,000 at the mid rate.

children.text: Measuring the Spread as a Cost
A spread in rupees means little until you compare it with the price. Express it as a percentage of the mid rate and you can compare any two channels, or any two currencies, on equal terms.

body.caption: The round-trip cost of buying and immediately selling back
Round-trip cost of $1,000 at each channel (mid 95.50)

body.text: A 3.66% round-trip cost is enormous by market standards. Many Nifty 50 index funds charge well under 0.5% a year, so one round trip on cash dollars costs more than seven years of those fees. That is why the unused dollars you bring back from a holiday are so expensive to convert: you paid the ask on the way out and get the bid on the way back.

body.title: The leftover dollars
body.prompt: After a trip to New York, Arvind has $300 in unused cash. He had bought it at 97.40, and the forex counter's buying rate today is 93.90. The mid rate has not changed. How many rupees does the round trip on these $300 cost him?
body.explanation: He paid 300 × 97.40 = ₹29,220 and gets back 300 × 93.90 = ₹28,170. The loss is ₹1,050, or ₹3.50 per dollar, entirely from the spread. Keeping a small balance on a multi-currency forex card for the next trip often costs less than converting back.

children.text: Pips: The Unit Traders Use to Measure Moves

markDefs.definition: Percentage in point. The standard small unit of movement in a currency pair: 0.0001 for most pairs and 0.01 for yen pairs.

children.text: Saying "EUR/USD rose by 0.0035" is clumsy, so global traders count in
pips

. For most pairs quoted to four decimals, one pip is 0.0001. For yen pairs, which are quoted to two decimals because a yen is worth so little, one pip is 0.01. A move in EUR/USD from 1.1600 to 1.1635 is 35 pips. A move in USD/JPY from 150.00 to 150.35 is also 35 pips.

body.caption: How moves are counted in different pairs

cells: USD/INR futures on NSE and BSE

body.title: Pipettes, fifth decimals and why the rupee is counted in paise

children.text: Many global trading screens now show a fifth decimal for EUR/USD (1.16003) and a third for USD/JPY (150.003). That extra digit is a pipette, one tenth of a pip. It exists because spreads in the most liquid pairs have become smaller than one pip.

The rupee market developed its own habit. Because USD/INR is quoted in rupees with two main decimals, Indian dealers, RBI commentary and newspapers talk in paise: "the rupee fell 12 paise." Indian exchanges then divide the paisa into quarters for trading, so the minimum price step on USD/INR futures is 0.25 paise. You will rarely hear an Indian dealer say "pips" about the rupee, but you will hear it constantly about EUR/USD.

body.title: Yen pip
body.textWithBlank: In USD/JPY, which is quoted to two decimals, one pip equals ___.
body.explanation: Yen pairs are quoted to two decimals, so the pip is 0.01. For most other pairs quoted to four decimals, a pip is 0.0001.

children.text: Turning Pips and Ticks Into Rupees

A pip or tick means nothing until you know how much currency you are trading. The rule is the same everywhere: the money value of a move equals the size of the move multiplied by the amount of base currency, and the answer comes out in the quote currency.

body.latex: \text{Profit or loss (in quote currency)} = \text{Price change} \times \text{Amount of base currency}
body.caption: Works for pips, paise and ticks alike

stats.context: One contract is on 1,000 US dollars

stats.label: Value of one tick per lot
Value of a ₹1 move per lot

children.text: Worked example: Rohit runs a small import business in Ludhiana and is hedging a dollar payment due next month. He buys 10 lots of USD/INR futures on NSE through Zerodha at 95.7225. The price rises 20 paise to 95.9225 and he sells at that level. Profit = 0.20 × $1,000 × 10 lots = ₹2,000, before brokerage and charges. The same 20 paise is 80 ticks, and 80 × ₹2.50 × 10 = ₹2,000. For a global comparison, a 35-pip move on €100,000 of EUR/USD is 0.0035 × 100,000 = $350.

body.title: Where is break-even?
body.prompt: Meenal imports electronic components into Noida and is hedging a dollar payment. She buys 5 lots of USD/INR futures at the ask of 95.7225, when the bid is 95.7200. Her total brokerage and charges for buying and selling will be ₹50. At what bid price must she sell to exactly break even? Give the answer to four decimals.
body.explanation: 5 lots = $5,000. To cover ₹50, the price must rise ₹50 ÷ 5,000 = ₹0.0100 above her entry: 95.7225 + 0.0100 = 95.7325. From the current bid of 95.7200, that is 1.25 paise, or 5 ticks: one tick to cross the spread and four to pay the charges. Every position starts in the red, so even a hedger who closes early has to earn back this gap before breaking even.

children.text: What Makes Spreads Wide or Narrow

columns.label: Spreads tend to be tight when
points: Lots of buyers and sellers are active, as in USD/INR during Indian market hours
You deal in a major pair such as EUR/USD or USD/JPY
You trade on a transparent exchange like NSE or BSE
You deal electronically in larger sizes
Markets are calm with no big news due

columns.label: Spreads tend to widen when
points: Liquidity is thin, such as right at the open or near holidays
Big events are due: RBI policy, US Fed decisions, US jobs data
You deal in a less-traded currency, such as Thai baht notes in India
You buy physical cash, which must be stored, insured and transported
Markets are panicking and dealers protect themselves

body.text: "Zero brokerage" does not mean zero cost. Every currency trade still pays the spread, plus exchange transaction charges, GST, stamp duty and SEBI fees. Offshore apps advertising "raw spreads from 0.0 pips" to Indian users are also not a legal route for residents, whatever their cost looks like. And since May 2024, rupee-pair contracts such as USD/INR on NSE and BSE may be used only to hedge a genuine currency exposure. Always calculate your all-in cost before you trade.

body.title: Paying the university
body.scenario: Ishita's family in Indore needs to pay $10,000 to a US university. They have three options. Option A: bank wire at a TT selling rate of 96.30 plus a flat ₹500 bank fee. Option B: load a forex card at 96.80 with no fee, then pay by card. Option C: buy cash at 97.40 and carry it. The mid rate is 95.50. Ignore GST and TCS.
body.prompt: Work out the all-in rupee cost of each option and the hidden cost compared with the mid rate. Which is cheapest, and what else should the family consider before choosing?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Option A: 10,000 × 96.30 = ₹9,63,000 + ₹500 fee = ₹9,63,500. Hidden cost vs mid (₹9,55,000) = ₹8,500.
2. Option B: 10,000 × 96.80 = ₹9,68,000. Hidden cost = ₹13,000.
3. Option C: 10,000 × 97.40 = ₹9,74,000. Hidden cost = ₹19,000, plus the risk of carrying cash.
4. Option A is cheapest by ₹4,500 over B and ₹10,500 over C, even after the fee. A flat fee is often smaller than a wider spread on large amounts.
5. Other points: universities usually want a wire to a specific account, so cash may not even be accepted; compare rates on CCIL's FX-Retail platform through their bank; ask about the university's own payment partners; and account for GST on currency conversion and TCS under LRS, which this exercise ignores.

body.title: Before any currency conversion or trade
steps: Find the current mid rate from a neutral source before you look at the dealer's quote.
Ask for both the bid and the ask, not just "the rate."
Work out the spread as a percentage of the mid rate.
Add every fee: bank charges, card fees, brokerage and exchange charges.
For trades, calculate your break-even move in paise or ticks.
Avoid dealing right before RBI policy, US Fed decisions or major data releases unless you must.

cards.definition: The price a dealer pays to buy the base currency. It is what you get when you sell.
The price a dealer charges to sell the base currency. It is what you pay when you buy.
Ask minus bid. The built-in cost of a round trip, and the dealer's margin.
The standard unit of currency movement: 0.0001 for most pairs, 0.01 for yen pairs.
The minimum price step on NSE and BSE: ₹0.0025, worth ₹2.50 per $1,000 lot.
How far the price must move in your favour to cover the spread and all charges.

points: Every quote has a bid and an ask. You buy at the ask, sell at the bid, and the headline mid rate is not a price you can trade at.
The spread is a real cost: about ₹3.50 per dollar for cash notes, ₹1.60 by bank wire, and a quarter paisa on NSE USD/INR futures in the example.
Compare channels using spread as a percentage of mid. A 3.66% round trip on cash is very expensive.
A pip is 0.0001 for most pairs and 0.01 for yen pairs. The rupee is counted in paise, and NSE and BSE futures move in ticks of 0.25 paise.
Money value of a move = price change × amount of base currency. One tick on one USD/INR futures lot is ₹2.50.
Every trade starts below break-even. Know how many ticks you need just to cover spread and charges.
Spreads widen around big events, at thin liquidity and for physical cash.
